summary: The note describes the Louisiana Purchase, the largest territorial gain in U.S. history, which doubled the size of the United States and stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains. It explains that France regained Louisiana from Spain in 1800 and sold it to the United States after failing to suppress the Saint-Domingue revolt and facing renewed war with Britain. It also covers the Federalist objection that acquiring territory was unconstitutional and Jefferson's argument that his treaty power was sufficient. The source text repeats the same passage twice, with the second version adding that the sale was meant to fund Napoleon's military.
one_line: The 1803 purchase of Louisiana from France that doubled U.S. territory, and the constitutional debate it sparked under President Thomas Jefferson.
key_facts: The Louisiana Purchase was by far the largest territorial gain in U.S. history.
The Louisiana Purchase stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains.
The purchase doubled the size of the United States.
Before 1803, Louisiana had been under Spanish control for forty years.
Spain aided the rebels in the American Revolutionary War but did not want the Americans to settle in its territory.
The Kingdom of France controlled the Louisiana territory from 1699 until it was ceded to Spain in 1762.
In 1800, French Emperor Napoleon regained ownership of Louisiana, hoping to re-establish an empire in North America.
France's failure to put down the revolt in Saint - Domingue, coupled with the prospect of renewed warfare with the United Kingdom, prompted Napoleon to sell Louisiana to the United States.
The Americans originally sought to purchase only the port city of New Orleans and its adjacent coastal lands, but quickly accepted the bargain.
The Louisiana Purchase occurred during the term of the third President of the United States, Thomas Jefferson.
The Federalist Party opposed the purchase, arguing that it was unconstitutional to acquire any territory.
Jefferson agreed that the U.S. Constitution did not contain explicit provisions for acquiring territory.
Jefferson asserted that his constitutional power to negotiate treaties was sufficient to make the purchase.
The second version of the passage says Napoleon, then First Consul of the French Republic, sold Louisiana to the United States to fund his military.
